# ggplot2 `coord_radial()` examples

`coord_radial()` is a modernised polar coordinate system introduced in
ggplot2 3.5.0. Compared with `coord_polar()` it adds three key capabilities:

- **Partial arcs** via an `end` argument (any arc from a sliver to a full circle).
- **Inner radius** (`inner_radius`) to create donut and gauge charts.
- **Radial-axis placement** (`r_axis_inside`) and optional angle-aesthetic
  rotation (`rotate_angle`).

The examples below are adapted from the
[ggplot2 reference page](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_radial.html).

```{python}
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import plotnine_polars as p9
from plotnine.data import mtcars
from plotnine_polars import aes
```

```{python}
mtcars_pl = (
    pl.from_pandas(mtcars)
    .with_columns(
        pl.lit("1").alias("x"),
        pl.col("cyl").cast(pl.Utf8),
    )
)
```

## Pie chart

A stacked bar chart becomes a pie chart under `coord_radial(theta="y")`.
This is the `coord_radial` equivalent of the `coord_polar` pie chart.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-pie
#| fig-cap: "Pie chart with coord_radial(theta='y')"
(
    mtcars_pl
    .ggplot(aes(x="x", fill="cyl"))
    .geom_bar(width=1)
    .coord_radial(theta="y", expand=False)
    .scale_x_discrete(expand=(0, 0))
    .scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    .add_theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```

## Coxcomb chart

A coxcomb (rose) chart maps each discrete category to an equal angular slice
but lets the bar *height* encode the count.  This is the default `theta="x"`
orientation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-coxcomb
#| fig-cap: "Coxcomb chart: bar heights encode count, angles encode category"
(
    mtcars_pl
    .ggplot(aes(x="cyl", fill="cyl"))
    .geom_bar(width=1, color="black")
    .coord_radial(expand=False)
    .add_theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```

## Bullseye chart

Swapping the aesthetics — stacking the cyl groups on a single x position with
`theta="x"` — produces concentric rings (a bullseye).

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-bullseye
#| fig-cap: "Bullseye chart: coord_radial() with a stacked single-bar"
(
    mtcars_pl
    .ggplot(aes(x="x", fill="cyl"))
    .geom_bar(width=1)
    .coord_radial(expand=False)
    .scale_x_discrete(expand=(0, 0))
    .scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    .add_theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```

## Donut chart

Setting `inner_radius` pushes data away from the centre, leaving a hollow
hole.  The value is a fraction of the outer radius, so `inner_radius=0.3`
creates a 30 % hole.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-donut
#| fig-cap: "Donut chart: inner_radius=0.3 carves a hole in the pie"
(
    mtcars_pl
    .ggplot(aes(x="x", fill="cyl"))
    .geom_bar(width=1)
    .coord_radial(theta="y", expand=False, inner_radius=0.3)
    .scale_x_discrete(expand=(0, 0))
    .scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    .add_theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```

## Pac-Man chart

Combining `theta="y"` with a non-zero `start` angle cuts a wedge out of the
pie.  A start of `π/3` (60°) creates Hadley Wickham's favourite illustration
of why pie charts are hard to read.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-pacman
#| fig-cap: "Pac-Man: coord_radial(theta='y', start=π/3)"
pac_data = pl.DataFrame({
    "variable": ["does not resemble", "resembles"],
    "value": [20, 80],
    "x": ["", ""],
})

(
    pac_data
    .ggplot(aes(x="x", y="value", fill="variable"))
    .geom_col(width=1)
    .scale_fill_manual(values={"does not resemble": "red", "resembles": "yellow"})
    .coord_radial(theta="y", start=np.pi / 3, expand=False)
    .labs(title="Pac Man")
    .add_theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```

## Partial polar scatter

Providing both `start` and `end` limits the plot to an arc rather than a
full circle.  Combined with `inner_radius`, this is the basis for gauge and
fan charts.  Here `mtcars` displacement is mapped to angle and fuel economy
to radius.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-partial
#| fig-cap: "Partial polar scatter: start/end define the arc, inner_radius adds a hole"
(
    pl.from_pandas(mtcars)
    .ggplot(aes(x="disp", y="mpg"))
    .geom_point()
    .coord_radial(start=-0.4 * np.pi, end=0.4 * np.pi, inner_radius=0.3)
    .add_theme(figure_size=(5, 5))
)
```
